stance_summary: The Fed held rates at 3.50-3.75% in July by a 9-3 vote, the most divided decision since 2016, with three regional presidents dissenting in favor of an immediate hike. Chairman Warsh delivered an unexpectedly hawkish Jackson Hole address emphasizing the 2% PCE target and calling financial conditions 'not restrictive,' pushing hike odds for September above 50%, though Governor Waller's more dovish September 3 remarks have since pulled odds back down. The committee is now sharply data-dependent on the delayed August CPI report (due September 11) just days before the meeting.
policy_outlook: The September 15-16 meeting will include a fresh Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot, the first since June, giving markets a clearer read on the committee's rate path. With inflation still running near 3.4% (July) and above the 2% goal for over five years, three sitting hawks (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) have publicly pressed for further tightening, while Waller and Williams say they could support a hold if the August CPI print confirms continued disinflation. A knife-edge outcome is likely: either a second consecutive divided hold or the first hike since the tightening cycle ended, with markets pricing roughly a coin-flip probability of a 25bp increase to 3.75-4.00%.
alert: August CPI (due Sept 11) lands just days before the Sept 15-16 meeting and is widely seen as the swing factor; FedWatch-implied hike odds have swung from ~37% to ~70% and back to ~48-59% within the past two weeks amid dueling hawkish (Warsh, Barr, Cook, Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) and cautious (Waller, Williams) commentary.

members.name: Kevin Warsh
members.title: Chairman
members.note: Warsh became Chair in May 2026 and has scrapped forward guidance, shrinking FOMC statements dramatically. His Jackson Hole speech was read as hawkish, recommitting to the 2% PCE target and calling financial conditions 'not restrictive,' though he has resisted signaling the September outcome, calling his approach 'deliberate ambiguity.'
members.latest_source: Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium keynote, August 28, 2026

members.name: Jerome Powell
members.title: Governor (Former Chair)
members.note: Powell stepped down as Chair in May 2026 but remains on the Board of Governors, with his governor term running until January 2028; he has kept a lower public profile on rate policy since the transition, focused on institutional matters including an ongoing investigation into the Fed's headquarters renovation.

members.name: John Williams
members.title: Vice Chair, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York
members.note: Williams shifted from firmly backing a hold to signaling openness to a September hike, saying there are 'no clear signs' current policy is sufficient to return inflation to target, while attributing the recent Treasury yield surge to AI-driven growth rather than inflation fear.

members.name: Michael Barr
members.title: Governor
members.note: Barr warned the Fed should be prepared to 'act decisively to raise rates' if inflation fails to moderate, noting price pressures have been above target for over five years, though he says his vote depends on incoming August data.
members.latest_source: Speech at the Second-Chance Lending Forum, September 1, 2026

members.name: Michelle Bowman
members.title: Vice Chair for Supervision
members.note: Despite a historically hawkish reputation, Bowman has penciled in multiple rate cuts this year citing labor-market fragility, though she has acknowledged that a prolonged Middle East conflict and persistent energy-driven inflation could shift her toward favoring tighter policy.

members.name: Lisa Cook
members.title: Governor
members.note: Cook said she is 'prepared to act' on a rate hike unless inflation data improves, stating she views inflation risks as currently outweighing employment risks in the Fed's dual mandate.

members.name: Philip Jefferson
members.title: Vice Chair
members.note: Jefferson has consistently framed policy as 'well positioned' while flagging upside inflation risks from tariffs and energy shocks, expressing support for holding steady but openness to hiking if disinflation stalls.
members.latest_source: Speech at Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, July 16, 2026

members.name: Christopher Waller
members.title: Governor
members.note: Waller pushed back on Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole tone, saying he would be 'inclined' to support a hold if the August CPI report (due Sept 11) confirms continued disinflation, though he would 'consider a rate hike' if inflation comes in hot.

members.name: Beth Hammack
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland
members.dissent_detail: Dissented at the July 2026 meeting, preferring a 25bp hike
members.note: Hammack has been the most vocal hawk, saying current policy 'isn't restrictive enough' and suggesting it may take more than a single quarter-point increase to bring inflation back to target.

members.name: Neel Kashkari
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis
members.dissent_detail: Dissented at the July 2026 meeting, preferring a 25bp hike
members.note: Kashkari has called for a gradual series of small rate hikes to address persistent supply shocks—including tariffs and AI-infrastructure spending—arguing early action could prevent the need for larger moves later.

members.name: Lorie Logan
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
members.dissent_detail: Dissented at the July 2026 meeting, preferring a 25bp hike
members.note: Logan has said rates should be 'modestly' higher and that the Fed cannot rely on an unexpected economic shock to bring down inflation, favoring proactive tightening.

members.name: Anna Paulson
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia
members.note: Paulson voted with the July majority to hold, calling it 'not a close call,' and estimates underlying inflation ex-shocks near 2.4-2.8%, but says a further hike 'remains a viable possibility' if progress on core inflation stalls.
